notes.text: Let no man's heart, &c. — It would have reflected upon his prince to say, Let not thy heart fail: therefore he speaks in general terms, Let no man's heart fail. A little shepherd, come but this morning from keeping sheep, has more courage than all the mighty men of Israel! Thus doth God often do great things for his people by the weak things of the world.
A youth — Not above 20 years old; and a novice, a raw and unexperienced soldier.

The Lord, &c. — The lion and the bear were only enemies to me and my sheep, and it was in defense of them I attacked them. But this Philistine is an enemy to my God and his people, and it is for their honour that I attack him.
armour — With armour taken out of his armoury. He seems to speak of some military vestments which were then used in war, and were contrived for defense; such as buff-coats are now.
Proved them — I have no skill or experience in the managements of this kind of arms.

Staff — His shepherd's staff. These arms in themselves were contemptible, yet chosen by David; because he had no skill to use other arms; because he had inward assurance of the victory, even by these weapons; and because such a conquest would be more honourable to God, and most shameful, and discouraging to the Philistines.
Drew near — Probably a signal was made, that his challenge was accepted.
Fair — Not having so much as the countenance of a martial person.
Dog — Dost thou think to beat me as easily as thou wouldst thy dog?

A God — Hebrew. that God, the only true God, is for Israel; or on Israel's side, and against you. Or, that Israel hath a God, a God indeed, one who is able to help them; and not such an impotent idol as you serve.

Saveth — That is, that he can save without these arms, and with the most contemptible weapons. The battle - That is, the events of war are wholly in his power. He will - David speaks thus confidently, because he was assured of it by a particular inspiration.
Drew nigh — Like a stalking mountain. Ran - So far was he from fear!
Forehead — Probably the proud giant had lift up that part of his helmet which covered his fore-head; in contempt of David and his weapons, and by the singular direction of providence.

glossa.text: *And he went. ((RAB. in lib. Reg.))* Allegorically, the Philistines are demons, etc., *as far as* they behead the uplifted Goliath, as it were, with his own sword.

notes.text: Thy name — Thy infinite power and wisdom, and faithfulness and goodness. The name of God is frequently put for God. Put their trust - The experience of thy faithfulness to thy people in all ages, is a just ground for their confidence.
Zion — Whose special and gracious presence is there. People - To the heathen nations.

Blood — The bloodshed of his innocent and holy ones: which though he may not seem to regard for a season, yet he will certainly call the authors of it to a severe account. Them - The humble, as it follows, or the oppressed, ver. 9, that trust in him, and seek to him, ver. 10, whom he seemed to have forgotten.

Gates — In the great assemblies. These gates he elegantly opposes to the former. Of - Of the people who live or meet together in Zion. For cities are as it were mothers to their people, and the people are commonly called their daughters. So the names of the daughters of Egypt, Jer. xlvi, 11, and of Edom, Lam. iv, 21, 22, and of Tyre, chap. xlv, 12, are put for the people of those places.
Higgaion — This is either a musical term, or a note of attention, intimating that the matter deserves deep meditation, or consideration, as the word signifies.

Forget — That do not regard God, nor his precepts, nor his threatenings and judgments. David complains of and describes the wicked, ver. 1-15. Prays to God to appear against them, and rejoices in the prospect of it, ver. 12-18.

glossa.text: « And he is become. » How great a thing it is, that he who is judge should be a refuge to the poor man, who desires nothing of the world. « In opportunities. » ((AUG.)) Man is not more opportunely turned away from the world, unless to these pleasures labours and sorrows be mingled.

« Let them hope. » ((AUG.)) When they cease to hope in the things of the world. Those turned away from the world, seeking where to fix their hope, the knowledge of the name receives. The name is known, when he whose the name is, is known. His name is Lord, which he knows who willingly serves him, or, who is, and therefore let no one hope in transitory things, which have nothing besides "it was" and "it will be." For what in them is to come, when it has come, straightway becomes past, it is awaited with desire, it is lost with sorrow, it is not held with certainty. « For thou hast not forsaken. » The prophet provokes the faithful to praise, looking upon the benefits of the present time and of the time to come.

« Sion. » ((Ibid.)) Contemplation, which is practised now, that we may come to the vision of peace, that is, from Sion into Jerusalem: but any zealous contemplation falls into error, unless the Lord dwell in it. « Pursuits. » ((HIER.)) That is, his commandments, upon which zeal is to be spent.

« For requiring. » ((Ibid.)) But as if they who are sent to evangelize should say, No one believes us, and we are slain, he answered: not without fruit, because « requiring in vengeance their blood, » in the judgment, where there shall be glory to the slain, punishment to the slayer: « he hath remembered, etc » ((Ibid.)) not after forgetfulness, but after a long time, according to the feeling of the weak, who think him forgetful, because it is not done so quickly as they wish: to whom also add, nay, he is not forgetful, as you think: and if I have said « he hath remembered, » this is against the complainers, who because of the delay think him forgetful.

« Have mercy. » ((CASS.)) In his own person he says what each one asks. « See. » ((Ibid.)) The look of God is help, and when it comes, the light also puts the darkness to flight: from the pride of the enemy is measured the humility of the sufferer, because these are humbled just so much as those are exalted.

« Who liftest me up from the gates of death, etc. » ((AUG.)) That is, from all covetous desires, by which one goes to death: death now is that very gladness in the enjoying of things desired; whence the Apostle: « A widow that liveth « in delights is dead ((I Tim. V)). » « In the gates of the daughter « of Sion. » They are all the best pursuits, etc., *as far as* which neither eye hath seen, nor ear heard. ((CASS.)) Gates against gates, because these are of death, those of life. « Sion. » ((Ibid.)) She begat all the Churches of the world, because there Christ was born, whence faith began.

« I will exult. » ((AUG.)) Thus far the cry, thereafter the Church which is afflicted says, I will exult in Jesus. ((CASS.)) For by hope she is saved. « In the snare. » ((Ibid.)) A hidden snare is a deceitful thought: the foot is the soul's love, which, if it be crooked, is called covetousness, if right, charity. For by it the soul is moved as it were to a place, whither it rejoices to have come by love. « In the snare » therefore, that is, in a fraudulent counsel: the foot, that is, the love which through fraud comes to a vain gladness, is caught, because that delight binds them, so that they dare not break off their love from thence and turn it to useful things. For if they should try, it is grief to leave the things which delight, and that grief does not suffer them to depart.
*He shall be known.* ((CASS.)) Or, of the judgment to come, etc., *as far as* as certain men falsely think.

*Let sinners be turned.* ((AUG.)) Here is the canticle of the diapsalma, as it were the hidden gladness of the separation: which is made here not by place, but by affection, between the good and the evil. ((CASS.)) To sinners with Antichrist he foretells the end of evils; as it were this meanwhile, but at last *they shall be turned,* lest they rejoice in their own things. *Into hell,* lest they think themselves to be sent elsewhere.
*Patience.* ((AUG.)) Patiently, for this chiefly will God be mindful of the poor, namely because of their patience.
*Arise.* ((AUG.)) He prays for the judgment to come. ((CASS.)) The prophet, speaking of the end of the world, foresaw the coming of Antichrist; whence as if terrified he cries: *arise.*
*Let them know.* That is, being tormented let them find by experience that they were foolish men.

notes.text: We then not only beseech, but as fellow-labourers with you, who are working out your own salvation, do also exhort you, not to receive the grace of God — Which we have been now describing. In vain - We receive it by faith; and not in vain, if we add to this, persevering holiness.

For he saith — The sense is, As of old there was a particular time wherein God was pleased to pour out his peculiar blessing, so there is now. And this is the particular time: this is a time of peculiar blessing. Isaiah xlix, 8.
Giving, as far as in us lies, no offense, that the ministry be not blamed on our account.

But approving ourselves as the ministers of God — Such as his ministers ought to be. In much patience - Shown,

1. In afflictions, necessities, distresses - All which are general terms.

2. In stripes, imprisonments, tumults - Which are particular sorts of affliction, necessity, distress

3. In labours, watchings, fastings - Voluntarily endured. All these are expressed in the plural number, to denote a variety of them. In afflictions, several ways to escape may appear, though none without difficulty in necessities, one only, and that a difficult one; in distresses, none at all appears.
In tumults — The Greek word implies such attacks as a man cannot stand against, but which bear him hither and thither by violence.

By prudence — Spiritual divine; not what the world terms so. Worldly prudence is the practical use of worldly wisdom: divine prudence is the due exercise of grace, making spiritual understanding go as far as possible. By love unfeigned - The chief fruit of the Spirit.

By the convincing and converting power of God — Accompanying his word; and also attesting it by divers miracles. By the armour of righteousness on the right hand and the left - That is, on all sides; the panoply or whole armour of God.

By honour and dishonour — When we are present. By evil report and good report - When we are absent. Who could bear honour and good report, were it not balanced by dishonour? As deceivers - Artful, designing men. So the world represents all true ministers of Christ. Yet true - Upright, sincere, in the sight of God.

As unknown — For the world knoweth us not, as it knew him not. Yet well known - To God, and to those who are the seals of our ministry. As dying, yet behold - Suddenly, unexpectedly, God interposes, and we live.

As sorrowing — For our own manifold imperfections, and for the sins and sufferings of our brethren. Yet always rejoicing - In present peace, love, power, and a sure hope of future glory. As having nothing, yet possessing all things - For all things are ours, if we are Christ's. What a magnificence of thought is this!

From the praise of the Christian ministry, which he began chap. ii, 14, he now draws his affectionate exhortation. O ye Corinthians — He seldom uses this appellation. But it has here a peculiar force. Our mouth is opened toward you - With uncommon freedom, because our heart is enlarged - In tenderness.
Ye are not straitened in us — Our heart is wide enough to receive you all. But ye are straitened in your own bowels - Your hearts are shut up, and so not capable of the blessings ye might enjoy.

Now for a recompence of the same — Of my parental tenderness. I speak as to my children - I ask nothing hard or grievous. Be ye also enlarged - Open your hearts, first to God, and then to us, so chap. viii, 5, that God may "dwell in you," 2 Cor. vi, 16; vii, 1; and that ye may "receive us," chap. vii, 2.

glossa.text: *Lest in vain.* The grace of God is the remission of sins, which he receives in vain who is not willing to exercise himself in good works, or who trusts in the things of the law.
*Now is the time.* Which was not in the old law, or, now, not tomorrow, not a year hence: because straightway, at the death of a faithful man: salvation is given.
*That it be not blamed.* Which would surely come to pass, if what we teach by word we did not show forth by the example of our work.

*As the ministers of God.* These do not flatter, as the false apostles do, being eager for gain. *In much patience, in tribulations.* Amid so many hard things the burden of Christ is light, and is rest, while within the Holy Spirit gives life and the hope of what is to come softens all things, for love makes all things savage and monstrous easy and well-nigh nothing. And according to this understand what is said: *Come to me, all you that labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you ((Matth. XI))*. And again: *Take up my yoke upon you, and you shall find rest to your souls. For my yoke is sweet ((Ibid.))*, etc.

*In chastity* being had, *in knowledge,* that all may know how to act chastely, and mingle in nothing of adulterate opinion. *In sweetness,* being had, *in the Holy Spirit:* that is to say, that they be sweet and affable according to God, not like those who by sweet discourses seduce the hearts of the innocent. *In charity not feigned.* That charity is feigned which forsakes in adversity.

*In the power of God.* Let us not hope in man or in goods; if there is anything of good, let us attribute it to God. Or he says this, because he who has the things aforesaid works miracles for the conversion of unbelievers.

*By glory and dishonour.* Let us show ourselves as the ministers of God. *By glory.* Whether we are glorious among men, or ignoble and despised, let us neither be puffed up thereby, nor thereby sink down or grieve. In the same way if we are defamed for some crime, or have a good repute for some work. Likewise let us show ourselves to God, held *as seducers* among some, which is false. And he does not say simply, *held seducers,* but adds: *as,* and thence comes the ill fame. And among others held as *true.* As if to say: this is true, yet let us neither be proud at a good esteem, nor grieve at a bad. Likewise held among others, *as chastised,* etc.

*As sorrowful.* The enemies thought that the apostles would not escape the threats of the wicked. They themselves, by the help of God, are safe from death present and to come. *Possessing all things.* Such are they who, casting away earthly riches, already hold the heavenly by faith. As having nothing they possess all things, who, keeping earthly things for use or for the work of mercy, hope that they shall one day have the heavenly riches. The glory of the apostles was to possess nothing at all, to be without care: and to possess both the things and the lords of them, because all things were laid at their feet.

*Our mouth.* As if to say: I have said many things about you, but all these, said amply and diffusely, look to your correction, O Corinthians, and not to my own pride; and so you are foolish, who have dismissed me.

notes.text: Matt. viii, 23; Luke viii, 22.
They take him as he was in the vessel — They carried him immediately in the same vessel from which he had been preaching to the people.
On the pillow — So we translate it, for want of a proper English expression, for that particular part of the vessel near the rudder, on which he lay.
Peace — Cease thy tossing: Be still - Cease thy roaring; literally, Be thou gagged.

glossa.text: *In the ship. ((BEDA.))* Allegorically: the sea, the surge of the age. The little ship, the cross, by which we mount the waves of the world and come to the shore of the heavenly country. Other ships, etc., *as far as* for those ships perhaps had lately been made and only brought down into the harbour, or had been brought back to harbour after the perils of the sea.

*In the stern. ((HIER.))* The stern with dead skins holds the living and keeps off the waves, and is made solid with wood, etc., *as far as: A great calm;* the peace of the Church after her afflictions, or the contemplative after the active life.

*Sleeping. ((BEDA.))* While the disciples are sailing Christ falls asleep, because, while the faithful are meditating on the rest of the kingdom to come and, by the favouring breath of the Holy Ghost or by the oarage of their own effort, are casting the waves of the world behind their backs, suddenly the passion of Christ comes upon them, and as he goes up, etc., *as far as* but let us run back to the pilot, let us diligently rouse him, who does not serve the winds but commands them, who will still all things, who will grant the harbour of salvation.

*Peace, be still.* Note that every creature feels the command of the Creator. Not that all things are animate, as the heretics lie, but that by the majesty of the founder the things which are insensible to us are sensible to him.

*Why are you fearful? ((BEDA.))* As if he said: Why do you fear while I am present? To which is like that which, after the resurrection, *he upbraided their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they who saw him rise again did not believe ((Marc. XVI))*. And again: *O foolish and slow of heart to believe in all things which the prophets have spoken! Ought not Christ to have suffered, and so to enter into his glory ((Luc. XXIV))*?

*And they feared.* Matthew: *But the men wondered, saying: What manner of man is this,* etc. ((Matth. VIII.)) Not therefore the disciples, but others who were in the ship, were wondering, doubting of him whom the sea and the wind obeyed. Or even the disciples themselves are rightly called men, because they did not yet know the power of the Saviour.

notes.text: Lord — The eternal word, Jehovah, the same who spake from Mount Sinai. Answered - Out of a dark and thick cloud, from which he sent a tempestuous wind, as the harbinger of his presence. In this manner God appears and speaks to awaken Job and his friends, to the more serious attention to his words; and to testify his displeasure both against Job, and them, that all of them might be more deeply humbled and prepared to receive, and retain the instructions which God was about to give them.

Counsel — God's counsel. For the great matter of the dispute between Job and his friends, was concerning God's counsel and providence in afflicting Job; which Job had endeavoured to obscure and misrepresent. This first word which God spoke, struck Job to the heart. This he repeats and echoes to, chap. xlii, 3, as the arrow that stuck fast in him.
Gird up — As warriors then did for the battle.
Where — Thou art but of yesterday; and dost thou presume to judge of my eternal counsels! When - When I settled it as firm upon its own center as if it had been built upon the surest foundations.
Measures — Who hath prescribed how long and broad and deep it should be. Line - the measuring line to regulate all its dimensions.

Foundations — This strong and durable building hath no foundations but God's power, which hath marvelously established it upon itself. Cornerstone - By which the several walls are joined and fastened together, and in which, next to the foundations, the stability of a building consists. The sense is, who was it that built this goodly fabrick, and established it so firmly that it cannot be moved.

Stars — The angels, who may well be called morning-stars, because of their excellent lustre and glory. Sons of God - The angels called the sons of God, because they had their whole being from him, and because they were made partakers of his Divine and glorious image. Shouted - Rejoiced in and blessed God for his works, whereby he intimates, that they neither did advise or any way assist him, nor dislike or censure any of his works, as Job had presumed to do.

Doors — Who was it, that set bounds to the vast and raging ocean, and shut it up, as it were with doors within its proper place, that it might not overflow the earth? Break forth - From the womb or bowels of the earth, within which the waters were for the most part contained, and out of which they were by God's command brought forth into the channel which God had appointed for them.

The cloud — When I covered it with vapors and clouds which rise out of the sea, and hover above it, and cover it like a garment. Darkness - Black and dark clouds. Swaddling band - Having compared the sea to a new-born infant, he continues the metaphor, and makes the clouds as swaddling-bands, to keep it within its bounds: though indeed neither clouds, nor air, nor sands, nor shores, can bound the sea, but God alone.

Break up — Made those hollow places in the earth, which might serve for a cradle to receive and hold this great and goodly infant when it came out of the womb. And set - Fixed its bounds as strongly as if they were fortified with bars and doors.
Gathered — Into their own land.

glossa.text:
*Give praise to the Lord.* ((ID.)) This psalm teaches what we are through ourselves, etc., *as far as* he first admonishes the redeemed to give praise. *Give praise.*

((CASS., AUG.)) Of which there are seven divisions, etc., *as far as* in the seventh he treats of heretics, there, *And they were made few.*
*And from the sea.* ((CASS.)) For the south he puts the sea, understanding thereby the ocean of that quarter; and this can be taken for any quarter of the world whatever.

notes.text: We then not only beseech, but as fellow-labourers with you, who are working out your own salvation, do also exhort you, not to receive the grace of God — Which we have been now describing. In vain - We receive it by faith; and not in vain, if we add to this, persevering holiness.

For he saith — The sense is, As of old there was a particular time wherein God was pleased to pour out his peculiar blessing, so there is now. And this is the particular time: this is a time of peculiar blessing. Isaiah xlix, 8.
Giving, as far as in us lies, no offense, that the ministry be not blamed on our account.

But approving ourselves as the ministers of God — Such as his ministers ought to be. In much patience - Shown,

1. In afflictions, necessities, distresses - All which are general terms.

2. In stripes, imprisonments, tumults - Which are particular sorts of affliction, necessity, distress

3. In labours, watchings, fastings - Voluntarily endured. All these are expressed in the plural number, to denote a variety of them. In afflictions, several ways to escape may appear, though none without difficulty in necessities, one only, and that a difficult one; in distresses, none at all appears.
In tumults — The Greek word implies such attacks as a man cannot stand against, but which bear him hither and thither by violence.

By prudence — Spiritual divine; not what the world terms so. Worldly prudence is the practical use of worldly wisdom: divine prudence is the due exercise of grace, making spiritual understanding go as far as possible. By love unfeigned - The chief fruit of the Spirit.

By the convincing and converting power of God — Accompanying his word; and also attesting it by divers miracles. By the armour of righteousness on the right hand and the left - That is, on all sides; the panoply or whole armour of God.

By honour and dishonour — When we are present. By evil report and good report - When we are absent. Who could bear honour and good report, were it not balanced by dishonour? As deceivers - Artful, designing men. So the world represents all true ministers of Christ. Yet true - Upright, sincere, in the sight of God.

As unknown — For the world knoweth us not, as it knew him not. Yet well known - To God, and to those who are the seals of our ministry. As dying, yet behold - Suddenly, unexpectedly, God interposes, and we live.

As sorrowing — For our own manifold imperfections, and for the sins and sufferings of our brethren. Yet always rejoicing - In present peace, love, power, and a sure hope of future glory. From the praise of the Christian ministry, which he began chap. ii, 14, he now draws his affectionate exhortation. O ye Corinthians — He seldom uses this appellation. But it has here a peculiar force. Our mouth is opened toward you - With uncommon freedom, because our heart is enlarged - In tenderness.
Ye are not straitened in us — Our heart is wide enough to receive you all. But ye are straitened in your own bowels - Your hearts are shut up, and so not capable of the blessings ye might enjoy.

Now for a recompence of the same — Of my parental tenderness. I speak as to my children - I ask nothing hard or grievous. Be ye also enlarged - Open your hearts, first to God, and then to us, so chap. viii, 5, that God may "dwell in you," 2 Cor. vi, 16; vii, 1; and that ye may "receive us," chap. vii, 2.

glossa.text: *Lest in vain.* The grace of God is the remission of sins, which he receives in vain who is not willing to exercise himself in good works, or who trusts in the things of the law.
*Now is the time.* Which was not in the old law, or, now, not tomorrow, not a year hence: because straightway, at the death of a faithful man: salvation is given.
*That it be not blamed.* Which would surely come to pass, if what we teach by word we did not show forth by the example of our work.

*As the ministers of God.* These do not flatter, as the false apostles do, being eager for gain. *In much patience, in tribulations.* Amid so many hard things the burden of Christ is light, and is rest, while within the Holy Spirit gives life and the hope of what is to come softens all things, for love makes all things savage and monstrous easy and well-nigh nothing. And again: *Take up my yoke upon you, and you shall find rest to your souls. For my yoke is sweet ((Ibid.))*, etc.

*In chastity* being had, *in knowledge,* that all may know how to act chastely, and mingle in nothing of adulterate opinion. *In sweetness,* being had, *in the Holy Spirit:* that is to say, that they be sweet and affable according to God, not like those who by sweet discourses seduce the hearts of the innocent. *In charity not feigned.* That charity is feigned which forsakes in adversity.

*In the power of God.* Let us not hope in man or in goods; if there is anything of good, let us attribute it to God. Or he says this, because he who has the things aforesaid works miracles for the conversion of unbelievers.

*By glory and dishonour.* Let us show ourselves as the ministers of God. *By glory.* Whether we are glorious among men, or ignoble and despised, let us neither be puffed up thereby, nor thereby sink down or grieve. In the same way if we are defamed for some crime, or have a good repute for some work. Likewise let us show ourselves to God, held *as seducers* among some, which is false. And he does not say simply, *held seducers,* but adds: *as,* and thence comes the ill fame. And among others held as *true.* As if to say: this is true, yet let us neither be proud at a good esteem, nor grieve at a bad. Likewise held among others, *as chastised,* etc.

*As sorrowful.* The enemies thought that the apostles would not escape the threats of the wicked. They themselves, by the help of God, are safe from death present and to come. *Possessing all things.* Such are they who, casting away earthly riches, already hold the heavenly by faith. The glory of the apostles was to possess nothing at all, to be without care: and to possess both the things and the lords of them, because all things were laid at their feet.

*Our mouth.* As if to say: I have said many things about you, but all these, said amply and diffusely, look to your correction, O Corinthians, and not to my own pride; and so you are foolish, who have dismissed me.

lines: The Lord is a stronghold for the oppressed, a refuge in trouble.
Those who know your name put their trust in you.
The wind howled and the waves broke into the boat.
And Jesus rose and said: Peace. Be still.
We come with sword and spear too small for our giants.
We come in the name of the Lord of hosts.
Come, let us worship the God who calms the sea.
We come, and we are not afraid. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Night on the water, the waves breaking over the side, the boat already filling, and you wonder if the One asleep in the stern even cares.
Peace. Be still.
Whatever giant stands over you, taller and louder than your faith, remember the boy who ran at it with five smooth stones and the name of God.
Peace. Be still.
The Lord is a refuge for the crushed, a stronghold in the time of trouble; the storm has never once had the last word.
Peace. Be still.
So come into the boat, all of you who are afraid; the wind drops, the sea goes glassy, and a great calm settles over the water.
Peace. Be still, and know that God is here.
